ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory risk-based screening under PCMLTFA and Criminal Code against: (a) consolidated United Nations Security Council sanctions lists implemented in Canada via the United Nations Act, SC 1991, c 45 and regulations (e.g., United Nations Suppression of Terrorism Regulations, SOR/2001-360); (b) Canadian autonomous sanctions regulations under the Special Economic Measures Act, SC 1992, c 17, the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Sergei Magnitski Act), SC 2017, c 21, and the Freezing Assets of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, SC 2011, c 22; (c) Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) and FINTRAC published lists and guidance; (d) Foreign terrorist entity listings under the Criminal Code (Decision No. 139-2012 and subsequent); (e) U.S. OFAC SDN List and sectoral/other sanctions lists as a prudent cross-border measure given CA-US interdependencies; (f) UN, EU, UK (HMT) and other allied lists for global onboarding and correspondent banking expectations. FINTRAC guidance (PCMLTFA and associated regulations) requires obligated entities to determine identity, conduct ongoing monitoring, and report suspicious transactions and attempted transactions. PEPs (domestic and foreign) and heads of international organizations must be subject to enhanced due diligence, including reasonable measures to establish source of wealth and source of funds; beneficial owners must be identified to the 25% tier (OBCA/CBCA) and FINTRAC beneficial ownership requirements adopted via the Regulations Amending the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations (SOR/2002-184 as amended, notably Definitions and Reporting requirements, effective in stages through 2024). Required screening of all named directors, officers, UBOs, and authorized signatories against all listed sanctions instruments prior to incorporation filings and before onboarding of the corporate bank account.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: For Ontario corporations: Ontario Business Central (https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-business-central) and the official Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Branch (CIPPSB) electronic search and filing services (Ontario Business Registry launched 2021). For federal corporations: Corporations Canada's online Name Reservation service via the Corporations Canada portal (https://www.ic.gc.ca/app/scr/cc/CorporationsCanada) using the NUANS Name Search System.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Ontario: Corporate name may be in English, French, or both, and may include other languages only if the name is also provided in an English or French transliteration using Roman letters; the corporate name's distinctive element must be expressed in letters of the Latin/Roman alphabet, Arabic numerals, or a combination, and the legal element (Limited, Limitée, Incorporated, Inc., Corporation, Corp., or the French equivalents) must be in the same language as the alphabet of the distinctive element; no concurrent use of more than one language for the legal element; for federal corporations under CBCA, the name may be in English, French, or a bilingual version; romanized transliteration of non-Latin script names is required; the NUANS report must accompany every name reservation and a proposed name must be distinguishable from all existing corporate, business, and trademark names, with the distinctiveness test applied under CBCA regulations (s. 18) and OBCA regulations (s. 5 et seq.). A prohibited name is one that is identical to or confusingly similar with an existing name; the name must not connotate the business of a person other than the proposed corporation, not suggest that the business is government-sponsored, and not contain an element subject to trademark protection confusing with a mark already in use.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Government (or any word implying government connection, e.g., Canadian, Toronto, Ontario or municipal names where misrepresentation may arise)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If a proposed name is rejected by the Ontario director (CIPPSB) or Corporations Canada, the applicant may submit a written request for reconsideration within the time prescribed by the applicable statute and regulations (Ontario: contact the Director under OBCA s. 9(6) and O. Reg 90/12; Corporations Canada: request a reconsideration of the NUANS examination and provide written representations addressing the examiner's concern). If the director refuses to permit a name, the corporation or applicant may apply to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice for an order directing the director to permit the name (OBCA s. 10(5)); for federal corporations, an appeal lies to the Federal Court under CBCA s. 12(4) (application by the applicant or corporation). Administrative steps: (i) obtain the written rejection notice or examiner's report; (ii) file a reconsideration request with the registry and include rebuttal evidence such as computed trademark search reports on the Canadian Trademarks Database, consent letters from existing name holders, or explanations of distinguishable elements; (iii) if the registry reaffirms the refusal, commence a court application. Parallel to a rejected reservation, an applicant may reserve a modified name immediately without prejudice. A name reservation may be extended by filing a renewal within the valid reservation period; the specific extension period is at the discretion of the Director under the applicable regulations, typically an additional 30-60 days.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Virtual office services are generally accepted in Ontario and at the federal level insofar as the registered office address is not a post office box and is a physical location in the jurisdiction where documents may be served (Ontario: OBCA s. 14(2), a registered office must be in Ontario at a specified street address; federal: CBCA s. 19(2), registered office must be in the province in which the head office is situated, at a place within that province capable of being specified accurately). In practice, registered agent offices and commercial virtual office suites providing a physical street address, document reception, and service-of-process arrangement are regularly used by AI/LLM API companies without physical premises. However, FINTRAC and the Canada Revenue Agency impose appropriate person/client identification requirements that may require the service provider to verify the corporation's management and place of business; banks and financial institutions (including Stripe and crypto/fiat rails) increasingly demand a real operating address or proof of commercial substance. For an AI/LLM API platform generating recurring cross-border revenue, the registered agent's address is permissible for registry purposes, but substantive bank onboarding (USDC via crypto-exchanges and Stripe merchant account) will generally require disclosure of an operating address, website traffic, and transaction history; purely virtual offices are accepted at incorporation but physical presence is recommended for obtaining a full-service corporate bank account.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low but nonzero. Ontario Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement and Corporations Canada do not generally conduct routine unannounced physical inspections of registered offices for standard ISIC 6201 AI/LLM API service corporations. The CRA may verify business existence and substance through correspondence and, in cases of GST/HST registration, international non-resident registrant scenarios, or suspicious refund claims, may request production of books and records; CRA field audits are typically announced. Financial institutions and crypto-fiat payment processors (e.g., Stripe, Coinbase Commerce/Exchange, and ancillary money services businesses) may conduct virtual or physical verification under AML/CFT rules, but unannounced physical on-site inspections are rare for a low-risk standard company. Estimated likelihood: less than 10% within the first three years for a registered-office-only company; materially higher if the corporation engages in regulated financial activity or claims input tax credits disproportionately. The federal and Ontario registries maintain powers to inspect records and may require the corporation to provide the registered office address; failure to maintain a registered office in Ontario at an address accessible for service is an offence under OBCA s. 14 and CBCA s. 19.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Number (BN) and GST/HST registrations under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act; portal: https://www.canada.ca/en/services/taxes/business-taxes.html; Ontario provincial registrations are integrated through the Ontario OneStop Business Registry (https://www.ontario.ca/page/one-stop-business-registry) and administered by the Ontario Ministry of Finance.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A CBCA-incorporated federal corporation is a Canadian-resident taxpayer and must obtain a CRA Business Number (BN), with program accounts for corporate income tax (RC) and GST/HST (RM). A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada or making Canadian supplies may also need a BN and GST/HST account. Procedure: (1) file Form RC1FF or complete online registration through CRA Business Registration Online; (2) provide articles of incorporation, registered office information, by-laws, and officer identification for a federal/provincial corporation; (3) for Ontario, register through the OneStop Business Registry to obtain Ontario corporate tax, Employer Health Tax, and other provincial accounts; (4) receive the 9-digit BN and subsequent 15-digit program account numbers; typical turnaround is 1-5 business days if fully electronic, with possible wait times for non-resident applications.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation – the Canadian entity is taxable in Canada on worldwide income as a separate taxpayer; it is not a pass-through for Canadian federal and Ontario tax purposes. A Canadian-resident corporation pays federal corporate income tax plus Ontario provincial corporate income tax; if it qualifies as a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), it may access the small business deduction. Non-resident shareholders are generally not deemed to carry on business solely by receiving dividends, but the corporation must withhold non-resident tax on dividends, interest, and royalties.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not adopt the U.S. check-the-box regime. Relevant elections include: (a) GST/HST closely related corporation election under ETA s.156, allowing taxable supplies between parent and 90%-owned subsidiary to be treated as nil for GST/HST; (b) ETA s.265 election for financial institutions in special situations; (c) income tax elections under s.85 or s.97 for tax-deferred transfers of property to a corporation or partnership; (d) an election under ETA s.272.1 for imported services or intangibles treated as supply made in a different place. For hybrid mismatch concerns, no domestic entity classification election is available; Canada's anti-hybrid rules in the Income Tax Act (s.18.4) and OECD MLI treaty application must be assessed based on the foreign entity's legal classification.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act; Ontario applies a harmonized value-added tax with Quebec and Atlantic provinces being separate regimes. In Ontario, GST (5%) and provincial HST (8%) are combined into a single 13% HST for most taxable supplies.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 – the small-supplier threshold for GST/HST registration. A Canadian-resident business must register when its worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies but excluding supplies that are taxable at 0%? actually zero-rated supplies are included in the threshold calculation) exceed CAD 30,000 in the last four consecutive calendar quarters or in a single calendar quarter. A non-resident carrying on business in Canada applies the same CAD 30,000 threshold with respect to its taxable supplies made in Canada. If the non-resident does not carry on business in Canada but makes online sales to Canadian consumers, it must nevertheless register and collect GST/HST once Canadian sales exceed CAD 30,000 unless the supplier falls under a special cross-border digital services rule; registration may be voluntary to recover input tax credits.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not mandate real-time fiscal clearance, transaction-level API filing, or digital stamping for GST/HST. Electronic invoicing is voluntary, though CRA requires electronic GST/HST return filing and remittance for registrants with taxable revenue above CAD 1 million (GST/HST electronic remittance). The PEPPOL network is being adopted in Canada but remains a private-sector convention, not a statutory compliance requirement. Invoices must contain the supplier's BN, date, supplier name and address, recipient name, description, amount and tax rate/tax paid, and are accepted in PDF or structured digital format. There is no CRA pre-authorization of invoice format or real-time tax nexus declaration.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available for exported goods under ETA s.22 and Schedule VI, Part V, provided the exporter has proof of physical export from Canada. For services, including generative AI / LLM API access, zero-rating applies when the service is supplied to a non-resident recipient who is not registered for GST/HST in respect of that service and the service is for consumption or use wholly outside Canada (ETA s.143 and place-of-supply rules). A Canadian supplier exporting AI APIs to a non-resident business or consumer should retain the contract evidencing non-resident ordering, the foreign payment method, and technical data showing the API token is consumed outside Canada. If the supply is made to a Canadian GST/HST registrant, or the service is delivered to a recipient resident in Canada, 13% HST applies unless another special rule applies. Canada does not impose a statutory 180-day foreign-currency repatriation deadline for GST/HST zero-rating; the 180-day figure in this dossier is used as an internal documentary reconciliation backstop to ensure payment and export evidence are contemporaneous.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Form B13 – Canada Export Declaration (submitted electronically through the Canadian Export Reporting System / CBSA portal for physical goods; not required for services or digital API supply)
Commercial invoice / signed SaaS or API service agreement referencing the non-resident customer and delivery jurisdiction
Proof of export conveyance for goods: bill of lading, air waybill, express courier receipt, or postal documentation showing export from Canada
Proof of payment from abroad: foreign bank statement, SWIFT/FX confirmation, wire transfer record, or regulated cryptocurrency settlement record (USDC) demonstrating the non-resident source of funds
Technical delivery evidence for AI/LLM services: API usage logs, server session records, IP origin logs, and a statement by the customer confirming access and use wholly outside Canada
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA will deny zero-rating and reassess at 13% HST plus statutory interest if export documentation is insufficient or the place-of-supply evidence does not establish non-resident use. Normal GST/HST reassessment limitation is four years from the date of assessment; this limitation does not apply where the supplier has made a misrepresentation or committed fraud. Civil penalties under ETA s.280 include 25% of net tax for a first false statement and 50% for a repeated false statement; gross negligence penalties under ITA s.163(2) can be 50% of understated income/benefit, and serious tax evasion may trigger prosecution with 50%-200% penalties and imprisonment. Records must be retained for at least six years after the fiscal year to which they relate; failure to retain records may support an unlimited reassessment and additional penalties under ETA s.284 and ITA s.230.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) is the central bank, with the Department of Finance Canada retaining exchange-control policy authority and the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) supervising the domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs). Canada repealed its Foreign Exchange Control Act in 1951; no federal agency issues exchange-control approvals today. The Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre (FINTRAC) administers cross-border currency and virtual-currency reporting under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), while Payments Canada operates the clearing and settlement infrastructure (Lynx, ACSS, and the Retail Payment Activities Act registration regime managed by the Bank of Canada).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible and floats freely. Current-account items (API subscription revenue, royalties, interest, dividends) and capital-account items (equity subscription, shareholder loans, capital reductions, buybacks) are exchange-free with no Bank of Canada or FINTRAC pre-approval requirement. Profit remittance frictions arise solely from tax law: Part XIII non-resident withholding tax (statutory 25%, reduced under the Canada-China Income Tax Agreement to 10% dividends for a company beneficially owning at least 10% of voting power, 15% otherwise; interest 10%; royalties 10%). Greenfield Ontario incorporation and subsequent operating remittances are not subject to Investment Canada Act net-benefit review; only acquisitions of control of an existing Canadian business above the WTO enterprise-value threshold trigger that review, and the national-security regime is fact-specific.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable. Canada maintains no statutory timeline, mandatory conversion ratio, or repatriation obligation for export proceeds. The Ontario AI-LLM API corporation may retain USD, USDC, and other foreign currency offshore or in domestic foreign-currency accounts. The only obligations are statistical reporting (Statistics Canada services-export surveys) and FINTRAC reporting for electronic funds transfers or large virtual-currency transactions individually at or above CAD 10,000.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-to-Medium. Canada does not recognize the UK/EU EMI licence; a foreign EMI cannot take deposits or maintain customer payment accounts in Canada without a Schedule I/II bank licence or a provincial trust-company licence. Offshore digital EMIs may only act as payment facilitators, not as the treasury ledger bank. Fintech rails (Stripe, Wise for Business) are viable for disbursements, card acquiring, and USDC conversion settlement, but the capital escrow ledger and core operating balances must remain at a Schedule I Tier-1 bank. Under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA, in force November 1, 2024; Bank of Canada registration transitional into 2025), the Ontario entity should require its processors to evidence FINTRAC MSB/VASP and RPAA registrations before contracting; no direct deposit-accepting function may be performed by an unlicensed foreign EMI.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote account opening is permitted by RBC, TD, BMO, and CIBC where at least one resident Canadian director (OBCA/CBCA requirement: 25% of the board resident Canadians, minimum one where the board has fewer than four directors) executes the application and completes video-verified KYC. Required documents: certified notarized Articles of Incorporation, By-Laws, Notice of Directors (Ontario Form 1), directors' consent/resignation registers, banking resolution, and beneficial-ownership register. Physical branch attendance is mandatory when the primary signing officer is a non-resident lacking a Canadian photo ID, or when the package includes USD cheques, a credit facility, or a documentary-credit line. For a low-risk ISIC 6201 software entity, a face-to-face English or French video interview satisfies customer-identification requirements without an in-person appearance.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cryptocurrency and USDC receipts in the revenue model triggering suspicion of unlicensed MSB/VASP activity
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Legal opinion confirming the corporation does not deal in virtual currency as a business under PCMLTFA; FINTRAC registration certificates of all payment processors and virtual-currency exchangers; treasury policy requiring same-day conversion to fiat through arm's-length regulated venues; complete blockchain transaction trail and wallet ownership records; automated sanctions screening against OFAC and Canadian CFSP/FSL lists.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Frequent cross-border wires to related parties or a foreign IP-holding group with heightened jurisdictional exposure
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed SDK/API licensing, royalty, and sub-license agreements; CRA Form T106 and OECD-aligned transfer-pricing benchmark documentation; commercial invoices carrying ISO 20022 purpose codes (ROYA or TRADE); SWIFT payment rationale memoranda; intra-group cost-sharing model evidencing arm's-length economics.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident director majority or apparent absence of Canadian commercial substance
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: OBCA/CBCA-compliant director slate with Form 1 Notice of Directors; statutory declarations of residency and proof-of-address for each resident Canadian director; Ontario head-office lease, payroll records, and customer contracts establishing a fixed establishment and genuine business activity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Opaque source of injected capital (nil minimum capital, shareholder funds sourced from crypto gains or foreign wealth)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Share subscription agreement and securities ledger; 6-12 months of shareholder bank or exchange statements; source-of-wealth statutory declaration; Ontario counsel escrow or trust accounting records; chain-of-title evidence for the subscription consideration; CRA corporate registration confirmation.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Repetitive low-value token-based invoicing to dispersed counterparties perceived as invoice fraud or laundering micro-structures
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Standard AI-API terms of service with metered token economics; Master Services Agreements with the twenty largest customers; representative invoice sample; API access logs evidencing consumption; documented refund and financial-crime escalation policy; submission of the full revenue model narrative to the bank's suspicious-transaction review unit.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Capital injections must arrive by SWIFT MT103 (or ISO 20022 message formats where supported) into the designated Capital Escrow or operating account at an Ontario branch of a Schedule I bank. The remittance instruction must name an explicit ExternalPurpose in the remittance information field, e.g., ECEQ for equity contribution, INTE for shareholder-loan advances, or DIVD where a pre-closing dividend is restructured; the bank requires the subscription agreement, corporate resolution, beneficial-ownership statement, and source-of-funds evidence before posting. CAD settlement clears through Payments Canada Lynx for high-value transfers; USD clears through CHIPS/Fedwire via the bank's New York correspondent. Individual cash or virtual-currency receipts at or above CAD 10,000 trigger FINTRAC large-cash or large-virtual-currency transaction reports, and all wires are screened against Canadian and global sanctions lists.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Operating disbursements (cloud compute, payroll, IP royalties, contractor fees) settle by SWIFT MT103 with the governing contract reference embedded in the remittance field; same-day CAD high-value payments clear via Lynx, while standard debit-credit flows use ACSS. For tangible procurement (GPU clusters, server hardware, data-centre equipment), the Ontario bank may issue an irrevocable documentary credit (SWIFT MT700) with 30-120 day tenor, requiring commercial invoice, bill of lading, or warehouse receipt. SWIFT gpi tracking is recommended for all outbound foreign wires. USDC revenue is liquidated through a FINTRAC-registered exchange and the fiat net proceeds are swept daily into the Tier-1 account to minimize FX spread, counterparty risk, and bank AML friction, while Stripe treasury rails handle card-acquirer settlement.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: OTC deliverable CAD/USD FX forward contracts under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement or a Schedule I bank proprietary FX trading master agreement
FX swaps on deliverable CAD/USD legs for liquidity and term-structure management
Long-dated cross-currency swaps (floating USD to fixed CAD) executed bilaterally with an OSFI-regulated dealer under ISDA credit support annexes
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) used only for illiquid emerging-market counterparty currencies; no NDF is used for CAD/USD because the Canadian dollar is fully deliverable
Exchange-traded CAD/USD futures and options on the Montreal Exchange (Bourse de Montréal) through a CIRO-regulated investment dealer for short-tenor hedging

USDC and bitcoin delta hedges (perpetual swaps or cash-settled options) permitted only through CIRO-regulated crypto trading platforms for treasury positions arising directly from token-receipt settlement; all hedge documentation maintained for OSFI and FINTRAC examination

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario Annual Return (OBCA s. 258) including Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) disclosure
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: ServiceOntario, Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, Province of Ontario
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within six (6) months after the corporation's fiscal year end; calendar-year filers must file no later than June 30
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Offence and fine up to CAD 1,000 under OBCA s. 258(4); administrative strike-off (dissolution by the Director without court order) after failure to file for two consecutive fiscal years under OBCA s. 241(2); restoration through ServiceOntario required to resume legal capacity.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (Federal and Ontario schedules integrated)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) acting as collecting agent for the Ontario Ministry of Finance under the Canada-Ontario Tax Administration Agreement
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within six (6) months after the fiscal year end; no extension is available for corporation filings
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of 5% of unpaid tax for the filing year plus 1% per full month of arrearage up to a maximum of 12 months; repeat-offender penalty of 10%; interest at CRA prescribed quarterly rate on unpaid balances; gross-negligence penalty up to 50% of understated tax under Income Tax Act s. 163(2).

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario Corporation Tax Return (T2CO / Ontario allocation schedules and corporate minimum tax provision)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) on behalf of the Ontario Ministry of Finance
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Filed concurrently with the federal T2: within six (6) months after fiscal year end
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Ontario tax arrears accrue prescribed-rate interest computed quarterly and are collected by CRA under the federal-provincial administrative agreement; same penalty architecture as federal returns applies to provincial balances.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T1135 Foreign Income Verification Statement (conditional: applies only if aggregate specified foreign property exceeds CAD 100,000 during the year)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annual; due with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return within six (6) months after fiscal year end
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Penalty under Income Tax Act s. 162(7): CAD 25 per day of delinquency, minimum CAD 100, maximum CAD 2,500; after formal demand, CAD 100 per day, minimum CAD 1,000, maximum CAD 24,000 under s. 162(7.02); possible denial of foreign tax credit relief upon reassessment.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No revenue-based audit threshold exists under the Ontario Business Corporations Act (OBCA). Offering (public) corporations must always appoint an independent auditor. A private non-offering OBCA corporation may be exempted from the auditor appointment only if all shareholders validly consent in writing each fiscal year; any shareholder holding 5% or more of the voting shares may compel an audit by written objection.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: CPA Canada Handbook: IFRS (Part I) is mandatory for public/offering enterprises; private Ontario corporations may elect ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises, Part II) or IFRS for financial reporting. Annual financial statements must be prepared, approved by the board of directors, and laid before shareholders at the annual meeting held within six months of fiscal year end (OBCA ss. 100 and 160).

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: OBCA s. 14.1 requires every private corporation to maintain an ISC register identifying every individual with significant control (25% or more of voting rights or 25% economic interest). Any share transfer that creates or terminates a significant control position must be recorded within 15 days of the corporation becoming aware; ISC particulars are reconfirmed annually as part of the Ontario Annual Return submitted to ServiceOntario within six months of fiscal year end. A share transfer is effective for voting and dividend entitlements only after registration in the Register of Members and Register of Transfers (OBCA ss. 86–87).
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 190–460 (CAD 250–600) per annum for a standard commercial registered office and corporate agent arrangement in Ontario
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 11,000–26,000 (CAD 15,000–35,000) for a full statutory audit of a technology/AI platform entity; USD 4,000–9,000 (CAD 5,500–12,000) for a review engagement where the shareholder audit waiver is validly in place

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 25% combined general corporate income tax (Federal Part I 15% + Ontario Corporate Income Tax 10%) for a Canadian corporation in Ontario without the small business deduction; 12.2% combined rate on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income of a Canadian-controlled private corporation (Federal 9% + Ontario 3.2%)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) investment tax credit: fully refundable 35% federal ITC for qualifying AI/LLM research expenditures up to CAD 3,000,000 per year (15% non-refundable beyond this cap); no Ontario provincial R&D credit currently available (repealed as of 2019); general rate reduction on federal income; Ontario small business deduction percentage; refundable dividend tax on investment income (RDTOH) integration.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal) with Ontario schedules, e-filed with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) using certified accounting/tax software via My Business Account, EDI, or GST/HST NETFILE; General Index of Financial Information (GIFI) balance sheet and income statement (Schedules 1 & 3) embedded in the T2.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end (ITA s. 150(1)); full balance of tax payable due 2 months after year-end (3 months for CCPCs claiming the small business deduction); companies are required to pay estimated federal and Ontario instalments quarterly (or monthly for large corporations) throughout the year for corporation-year ends after 2018.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total revenue: gross revenue from AI token metering and LLM API platform usage, subscriptions, setup fees and related services, recognized under IFRS 15/ASPE 3400 (For-profit entities must present financial information according to GIFI).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include revenue attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment (PE); revenue from fully offshore server locations and non-resident customers may be allocated using the CRA's PE apportionment rules; full supporting transfer-pricing documentation is required for the non-resident allocation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable dividends received: grossed-up taxable dividends from taxable Canadian corporations, eligible for the S. 112 deduction (100% for private corporations).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Dividends received from foreign affiliates must be traced through Schedule 21 (FAPI) and S. 90 inclusion rules, or treaty-exempted under S. 113.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total deductions: all business expenses (cloud compute, personnel, contractor fees, open-source licensing, token processing fees, depreciation) claimed as reasonable and arm's length.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses charged by a non-resident affiliate (e.g., central management, IP license fees) must satisfy the S. 247 arm's length standard and be documented before the filing due date.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income determined after applying S. 111 loss carryovers and the capital cost allowance system (CCA).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The taxable income of a non-resident-owned corporation is computed on the basis of Canadian-source business income only; no Canadian income for offshore PE income with no Canadian presence.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal Part I tax on taxable income: 15% general rate; 9% for the small business deduction attributable to Canadian-controlled private corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-CCPCs do not claim the small business deduction; the 'general rate reduction' produces the 15% federal effective headline rate.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal tax reductions: Small Business Deduction (Schedule 5), General Rate Reduction, Investment Tax Credits (SR&ED, S.127).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For federal-provincial allocation, the small business limit is allocated across permanent establishments using Schedule 6 (Ontario: CAD 500,000).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Ontario corporate income tax (OCT) payable, administered and collected by the CRA under the Ontario Corporate Tax Act: 10% general rate on active business income; 3.2% for Ontario small business income; no separate Ontario return.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Ontario tax is computed using the provincial allocation formula in Schedule 9 based on the Ontario permanent establishment's share of gross revenue and salaries.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial (Ontario) tax calculation and CCPC active business income determination, including refundable investment tax on portfolio income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Schedule 6/7 allocate each province's small business limit and the Ontario tax computation for a permanent establishment.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign tax credit for withholding tax paid on foreign royalty/interest, and FAPI for passive income in foreign subsidiary.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a Canadian taxpayer with US/EU API infrastructure, foreign source tax credits reduce Canadian tax on the same income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information return of non-arm's length transactions with non-residents (mandatory).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mandatory whenever aggregate cross-border transactions with non-residents exceed CAD 1,000,000, regardless of entity type.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: 5% of unpaid tax payable at the due date plus 1% for each complete month of delay, capped at 12 months (S. 162(1)); second-offense mis-filing: 10% + 2% monthly; gross-negligence penalty of 50% of the tax understatement (S. 163(2)); S. 161(1)/(2) interest compounded daily at the CRA prescribed rate; criminal fines of CAD 1,000 to CAD 25,000 (S. 238(1)) in obstruction or false filing cases.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form T106 - Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents, e-filed through CRA My Business Account.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due with the T2, six months after fiscal year-end.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Identify non-arm's length non-resident participants, transaction types, country of residence, aggregate transaction values and S. 247 methodology applied.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: List each related party informational transaction (loans, services, IP licenses, cost-sharing) including payments received and paid.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Transfer-pricing method selected (CUP, resale price, cost plus, TNMM, profit split) and explanation of comparability.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The method must be documented contemporaneously in the Master File format within the statutory due date.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Penalty of CAD 250 for each complete day of late filing, maximum CAD 32,500; in cases of knowing failure, penalties of CAD 500 to CAD 12,000, and imprisonment of up to 12 months (S. 238(1)).
